data.title: U.S. Stocks Extend Plunge as AI Boom Turns to Bust
data.description:
By Rob Curran

U.S. stocks plunged and an index of mega-cap technology stocks skirted bear-market territory as predictions of a speculative bust in artificial-intelligence stocks appeared to come to fruition.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48147.33. The broad S&P 500 dropped 265.44 points, or 3.70%, to 6910.39. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite sank 1261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22617.73, and came close to bear-market territory during the session.

The Nasdaq 100, a basket of the largest tech companies that is tracked by many tech-oriented investment and retirement funds, closed at 25028.98, almost 20% below its October peak, on the verge of bear-market territory.

Anthropic's shares tumbled 9.1% to $88.30 as fear of missing out on the Claude chatbot maker's IPO gave way to skepticism about its profit outlook. One strategist said market emphasis shifted this week from Anthropic's voracious demand for chips to its ability to translate that computing power to profits.

"They were telling us the narrative: 'we are going to print money with this compute,'" said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at money-management firm Equity Armor Investments. "We need this compute to figure it out, and eventually we'll grow into it, and AI is going to be something everybody needs, it's going to be the greatest thing in the world.'"

Now that Anthropic is public, Tigay said, the message from investors is: "'Show me, show me how this is going to turn into profit for you guys and eventually for the whole economy, thus lifting market higher.'"

At its low of the session, Anthropic came within 5 cents of its $83 IPO price and was down 28% from its Thursday peak.

Tigay said it was possible that the rout continued, mushrooming into something like the Dotcom bust or the 19th century railroad panic. But that still would not mean that AI would be remembered as a net negative for the U.S. economy, he said.

"Look at Amazon...they went public in the middle of that run and struggled for many years before really taking off and becoming a really profitable company," said Tigay. "It's possible Anthropic can go through that, and we'll look back and say they weren't making money yet but they had great leadership, a great product and they were just chugging away at it."

Write to Rob Curran at rob.curran@wsj.com

data.title: PMV Pharmaceuticals Reports 48% Response Rate in Ovarian Cancer Trial; NDA Planned for Q1 2027
data.description:
PMV Pharmaceuticals reported updated Phase 2 results for rezatapopt, showing a 48% response rate in platinum-resistant or refractory ovarian cancer and an NDA submission planned for the first quarter of 2027.

Key Highlights:

  • Among 65 ovarian cancer patients, confirmed ORR was 48%, with a median response duration of 10.4 months.
  • Across 168 evaluable patients in all cohorts, ORR was 36%, with a median response duration of 8.1 months.
  • Rezatapopt responses were reported across eight tumor types with TP53 Y220C-mutated, KRAS wild-type tumors.
  • Most treatment-related adverse events were Grade 1 or 2; individual Grade 3 event rates were no higher than 7.2%.
  • PMV plans to submit an NDA for platinum-resistant or refractory ovarian cancer in the first quarter of 2027.

data.title: Automakers sue NJ over vehicle warranty and recall repair law - Reuters
data.description:
Ford , Honda , Volkswagen , and Stellantis’ FCA unit  are suing New Jersey in an attempt to block a 7-month-old law that leaves automakers responsible for warranty and recall costs.

According to Reuters, the automakers claim the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Open Recall Notice and Fair Compensation Act gives franchised dealerships “unilateral and unchecked power” to charge “extortionate” prices for repairs that automakers are responsible for.  Manufacturers also argue that the statute prevents them from avoiding or recovering the added costs.

The New Jersey Motor Vehicle Open Recall Notice and Fair Compensation Act requires automakers to pay dealers at least 1.5% of a used vehicle’s value per month if recall parts are unavailable within 30 days of a stop-sale or do-not-drive notice until parts arrive or the vehicle is sold.

The law also sets rules for how automakers reimburse dealers for warranty and recall repairs, including labor rates, prices for parts, labor hours, and claim processing.

If the automakers are successful in their challenge, it would limit the reach of the current payment system for dealerships in the state. If the challenge fails, the plaintiffs claim the law gives dealers too much control over repair reimbursement.
